```text
Peak Poker Performance

   ♠ What physiological symptoms did you experience (heart pounding,

   ♠ What were the results or consequences of your reaction(s)?

   Whatever you determine, it’s important that you don’t get down on
yourself. A critical voice that becomes dominant and nasty will amplify
unpleasant feelings. A constructive critique can be helpful, but saying
things like “you’re so stupid!” to yourself is highly toxic and won’t serve
you in any way.

Reacting to Strong Emotional Responses
We’ve established that playing in the zone requires a level of emotional
detachment that is not always easy to achieve. Currently, we use the
word “tilt” as a catch-all descriptor for the myriad of non-useful emotions
that can come up while playing poker. Virtually everyone suffers from
some degree of tilt. While it usually lessens as a result of learning and ex-
perience, there are some psychological techniques you can use to reduce
it even further.
    A theory of psychotherapy called acceptance and commitment therapy
offers some practical (and empirically based) skills that can be used to
lessen emotions and unwanted thoughts.
    Our minds tell us “stories”, and we often react as if those stories are
100% true or we must give them 100% of our attention. This reaction is
known in psychological circles as “fusion.” When we are in a state of fu-
sion, we get caught up in our thoughts, and we will leap from the thought
to a conclusion. For example, if you are fused with the thought “I’m going
to fail,” you will behave as though failure is a foregone conclusion. When
we are in a state of fusion, it appears as though thoughts are reality and
that they are the truth. A natural reaction to fusion is to feel upset. So
how do you get rid of thoughts that are causing you grief?
    You can try a technique called “I’m having the thought that…” Bring to
```

```text
                                               Deconstructing the A Game

mind a thought that follows the form “I (am a loser; never win my flips,
etc.).” Preferably pick a recurring and upsetting thought. Focus on it, give
it your full attention, and believe it as much as you can for 10 seconds.
Next, take that repetitive and disturbing thought and insert the phrase
“I’m having the thought that” in front of it. For example, if you have the
thought that you will never win at poker, then think, “I am having the
thought that – I will never win at poker.” Think this over for a few sec-
onds, and notice how you feel. Now add to the phrase: "I notice that – I
am having the thought that – I am X.” For example, “I notice that – I am
having the thought that – I will never win at poker.” Think about that for a
few seconds, and then notice how you feel.
    Most people find that inserting those phrases gives them some dis-
tance. It’s as if you stepped back from your recurring, upsetting thoughts,
and when you do that, they have less power over you. It also interrupts
the emotional part of your brain (the amygdala), and gives your thinking
brain (the prefrontal cortex) time to come online, so to speak. The think-
ing brain is then able to think rationally and logically.
    You can use this technique with any of your negative or upsetting
thoughts so you are not at their mercy. You can step back and see them
for what they are – words that are passing through your mind. The mind
is a great story teller, and it tells you tall tales all day long like: “I’m not
good enough,” “I’m not smart enough to learn poker math,” “I’ll never win
again,” or “The poker gods are against me.”
    This technique is known as defusion; its goal is to help you realize that
thoughts are merely stories, words, or bits of sound. They may or may
not be true; they may or may not be important. They are definitely not
orders, and we don’t have to obey them. They do not represent any kind
of threat to you. The aim of defusion is not to get rid of the thought, per
se. Nor do you debate it or challenge it. You simply see and accept the
thoughts for what they are.
    Research shows that up to 80% of our thoughts contain some degree
of negative content. If you take these stories as truth, they can feed into
your anxiety, depression, self-doubt, anger, and/or insecurity. Having a
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

negative story is only a problem if you fuse with it. If you understand it is
just a story that’s separate from you and don’t give it your full attention,
it will cease to be a problem.
    Anytime you are feeling stressed or tilted ask, “What story is my mind
telling me right now?” Once you have identified it, you can defuse it. This
will allow you to put your full attention back where it belongs: on the
game.
    What if you have a negative thought that is true? In this method, it is
important to focus on whether or not the thought is helpful to you, at this
moment. If the words are helpful, it’s worth paying attention to them; if
not, address them later. If the thought demoralizes you, it’s not helpful.
The entire focus of acceptance and commitment therapy methods is
something called workability, which is determined by answering the ques-
tion: “Is what you are doing (or thinking) working to make your life rich,
full, and meaningful?” If yes, it is workable, and it makes sense to keep
doing it. If the answer is no, it is unworkable and you need to consider do-
ing something different. All recurring thoughts should be assessed by ask-
ing whether they help to create the life you want: if they do, fine; if they
don’t, don’t give them any weight.

Cognitive Defusion in Action
Let’s suppose you are in the midst of a terrible downswing and you tell
yourself that it will never end. To go through the process of defusion,
take the following steps:

   ♠ Analyze how the thought or belief that your downswing will never
       end affects you. How does thinking this way make you feel? How
       is it affecting your behavior at the table? Are you avoiding good
       games? Playing too tight? Feeling depressed?
   ♠ Is this way of thinking getting you the results that you want? Is it
       useful? Does it keep you from taking effective action? In other
       words, is this line of thinking workable?
   ♠ If it is not useful, can you change how you relate to the thought?
```

```text
Summary
Being able to manage yourself is not about controlling emotions as much
as about being open to your human feelings and strong emotions. It’s very
difficult if not impossible to purge or control emotions, consistently, for
any period of time. Most people want to eliminate tilt, but this is almost
always counterproductive. In their attempt to get rid of thoughts and
emotions, they end up struggling with them more. Their attention gets
diverted from the table and onto their internal state, which makes it im-
possible to stay in their zone of optimal performance. Your goal should be
to figure out ways to manage your thoughts, feelings, and behaviors so
that you can spend more time in your optimal zone of functioning.
   Your goal is to be balanced in your demeanor at the table. Don’t give
anything away. Calmly think through your decisions, and play all your
hands physically the same way. It doesn’t matter if you are holding pocket
kings or 36s, don’t freely give any information about your hand. Stay on
the same mental wavelength regardless of your cards.
   “Be balanced” not just in reference to the cards you play, but also in the
way you act. Try the exercises described above, if you find yourself getting
emotional. If you cannot control your emotions, you need to recognize
when they are getting out of hand. Are you starting to feel frustrated?
Anxious? Angry? Are you in a gambling mood and wanting to get your
money in? If you feel as if you’re getting run over and want to play back, take
a minute and realize that you are starting to get emotional and not thinking
clearly. You have to adapt – either manage your emotions or sit out.
   The solution is not to become a robot – you can’t get rid of emotions or
shut them down completely. It’s not healthy for life. Listen to them and al-
```

```text
Chapter Highlights
   ♠ The A game is by definition subjective and dynamic.
   ♠ It’s important to define your A through F game rating system, so
       that you recognize cues for taking necessary action.
   ♠ The brain is physically incapable of multi-tasking; the more
       frequently you switch tasks, the more mistakes you will make.
   ♠ Mature your A game by either adding new skills or eliminating
       errors.
   ♠ A flow state is also known as an optimal peak performance state.
   ♠ You can engage a flow state by learning to control your
       consciousness.
   ♠ Strong emotions, positive or negative, can adversely affect your
       game when you become mentally and emotionally hijacked by
       them.
   ♠ Becoming self-aware of your emotional responses is the first step
       to improvement.
   ♠ The “I’m having the thought that...” technique is used to defuse
       yourself from recurring and upsetting thoughts.
```

```text
                                              Deconstructing the A Game

game gets more difficult, you will find that your focus greatly determines
how successful you are. For example, no one will ever have an edge on me
at tic-tac-toe because the game is solved, but No-Limit Hold’Em is com-
pletely different.
   I know that when I am on my A game, I am constantly thinking about
what each and every bet size means. I am also vividly aware of my oppo-
nents’ physical tells. Decrypting bet sizing and physical tells can give you a
gigantic edge. If you are blind to them because you simply aren’t paying
attention, you are leaving a significant amount of money on the table.
While I am confident that I could beat any $10/$20 No-Limit game con-
sisting of a few pros and a few recreational players blindfolded, I would
have a much higher win rate if I could see my opponents. When I am not
focusing well, it is almost as if I lose the ability to analyze and decipher
their behaviors. Of course, some may say that I should spend more time
studying tells, but in reality, both tells and No-Limit Hold’Em strategy are
so deep that they simply cannot be fully mastered.
   When I find myself not playing my best, which I admit happens more
often than I would like, I usually stand up, stretch, order a cup of green
tea or coffee, and resolve to play my best. I challenge myself to pay at-
tention to the next hand as well as I possibly can, then challenge myself to
repeat the process on the next hand, and so forth.
   I have found that when I am tired I focus quite poorly, especially after a
night of partying. This is the main reason why I have resolved to get to
sleep early on the day before a tournament. I want to be as awake and
aware as I can possibly be. Preparing to play by getting into a serene state
of mind allows me to play my best, regularly.
   Another thing I have found that greatly increases my ability to focus is
to turn off my phone while I am playing. I turn it off and put it in my back-
pack. While I feel a bit naked without my phone in my pocket, having it
away from my body whenever I am seated at the table makes it much
more difficult for my mind to become distracted by a text, email, or Twit-
ter. It is unbelievable to me how many poker players refuse to be without
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

going on around you, you will focus better and be much happier.
    It is worth mentioning that there are two schools of thought when it
comes to approaching high stakes tournaments. Some players, myself in-
cluded, play almost every event of a specific buy-in level (usually $1,000
for me) and higher at each tournament stop. Others only play when they
wake up and feel as if they can play their absolute best. My “online kid”
mindset has led me to focus on putting in as much volume as possible,
even when I am not on my A game. However, there are many players who
have significant success only playing a few tournaments per trip. They
typically only play the larger events where they expect to have a large
hourly rate. By skipping the events with a low potential hourly rate, they
believe they show up more focused and refreshed when playing for the
big bucks. While I am not sure which approach is best, if you told me I
could either make $100 per hour playing 100 hours during a 10-day
poker trip or $300 per hour playing 30 hours, sign me up for the 30
hours! Sadly I have not put in the due diligence to say with any certainty
which approach is optimal for me.
    From years of self-analysis, I have discovered subconscious cues that
let me know when I am close to going on tilt. When I play online, I click my
mouse a bit harder than normal. When I play live, I put my chips in the pot
a bit more aggressively than normal. When I notice these actions, I make a
point to stand up and stretch, take a few deep breaths, and take a mo-
ment to be gracious for the amazing situation I am in (being able to play
the game I love). By noticing the first warning signs that tilt may be
around the corner, I am able to keep my emotions in check so they never
have a chance to alter my decision-making abilities. I suggest you observe
your actions and find your pre-tilt cues so you can better observe and
dismiss the onslaught of emotions that may be on their way.
```
